analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $9.80 over two years and indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 117 cosponsors, was sent to a House committee and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.10, then $8.95, then $9.80 in steps over two years. After that, the wage would rise automatically each year with the cost of living, so Congress would not have to keep voting to raise it. It also raised the cash wage for tipped workers, like waiters, toward 70% of the full minimum wage, up from $2.13 an hour, and required the Labor Department to publish each increase 60 days before it took effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage and tipped workers such as waiters and bartenders. About 3.6 million workers earned at or below the federal minimum when the bill was introduced, most of them adults in food service, retail, and other low-wage jobs [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps: $8.10 two months after enactment, $8.95 a year later, and $9.80 two years later [S2][S3].
After two years, the wage would rise each year with the Consumer Price Index, so it would no longer lose value to inflation between congressional raises [S2][S3].

Raises the tipped minimum wage from $2.13 to $3.00, then brings it to 70% of the full minimum wage over several years, directly boosting cash pay for waiters and bartenders whose tips alone often fall short [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that pay minimum or near-minimum wages, especially restaurants, fast food, retail, and hospitality, through higher payroll costs. Some of that cost would be passed to customers through prices; small businesses operating on thin margins would feel it most.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face higher labor costs at each step, and small businesses in low-margin industries would bear these increases on top of paying 70% of the full minimum wage in cash to tipped staff before tips [S2][S3].

Opponents of minimum wage increases generally argue that higher mandated wages can lead some employers to raise prices, cut hours, or hire less; the bill's sponsors did not include any offsetting relief, such as small-business tax credits, for employers absorbing the higher costs.

The bill's increases phased in over two years, so the final $9.80 wage was lower than what later proposals sought, and workers making slightly above the new minimum would get no direct raise even as costs around them rose [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of workers earning $7.25 an hour, the gains are direct and certain: a raise of up to $2.55 an hour and a tipping floor several times higher than the existing $2.13. The costs fall on employers and partly on customers through prices. Economists debate how much modest minimum wage increases reduce hiring; a stepwise increase spread over two years, as this bill proposed, is a design most studies find less disruptive than a sudden jump. The bill's main weakness is that it offered no offsetting help to the smallest employers facing the largest proportional cost increases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative George Miller, the senior Democrat on the Education and the Workforce Committee, introduced the bill on July 26, 2012, with 117 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, controlled at the time by Republicans [S5].
Two months later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the last action ever taken on the bill; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died without a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers, especially restaurants and retailers, kept paying the $7.25 wage (unchanged federally until 2007-2009 raises stopped there) and the $2.13 tipped wage, avoiding the higher payroll costs the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA), senior Democrat on the Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage to $9.80 with inflation indexing and a higher tipped wage.

for.name: 117 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors from the House Democratic caucus
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-strength sponsorship in the 435-member House.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on the minimum wage bill, leaving it in the Workforce Protections subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring any minimum wage increase to the House floor during the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 117 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee and House floor never took the bill up [S4][S5].

industries.note: Restaurants would pay $3.00 per hour in cash to tipped staff, rising to 70% of the full minimum wage, up from $2.13, plus higher wages for other staff. This industry employs the largest share of tipped and minimum-wage workers, so its labor costs would rise the most.
These industries employ many workers at or near the minimum wage and would face payroll increases in each step of the schedule, partly offset by workers having more money to spend.
